Rita was wandering in the shopping mall, looking for a gift for her little daughter. Suddenly she stopped before {{1}} store, as if drawn by something invisible. There were all kinds of dolls in it, their glass eyes shining under the warm light.

"Why not {{2}} her a lovely doll? Girls like dolls," she thought as she stepped inside, her mind drifting back to her own childhood.

{{3}} looking around, she saw a grandma doll — one with gray hair and a pair of glasses. As she looked at it, in her mind was Linda, her mother.

When Rita was a little girl, she got her first doll from Linda for her birthday. She was very happy. Then the second, the third... Rita asked her mum {{4}} all the gifts were dolls. Her mother would look at her for a moment, then smile and say, "A girl can never have enough dolls." Year after year, Rita grew up and Linda grew old, but a doll a year from Linda never arrived late.

"But why always a doll?" This question stayed in Rita's mind, like a seed waiting to sprout. One day her father gave the answer.

Little Linda dreamed to have a doll. Her parents promised {{5}} for her fifth birthday. {{6}}, they both died in a traffic accident before it arrived. The doll was the last thing they had promised her. It was not just a toy, but a reminder of her parents' love. The never-received gift was {{7}} than any other gift in her eyes. That's why she gave a doll as a present for Rita every year.

Then Rita got an idea...

It was Linda's {{8}} birthday. Much to Linda's surprise, she got a gift, with a card:

Dear Linda,
I {{9}} to send you the package that you should have received on May 20, 1956, your fifth birthday. The gift inside has aged, but I felt that you might still wish to have it. Sorry for the lateness!
Love,
Angel of Joy

Linda opened the package and saw a lovely grandma doll. She held tightly the doll that she had waited for so many years, tears running down her face. The doll, given by "Angel of Joy", made her the {{10}} "child" in the world.

passages.阅读理解 (A):
Should students be allowed to use smartphones in school? This question has been debated for years. Recently, several countries — including France, China, and parts of the UK — have introduced bans (禁令) on phones in primary and secondary schools. But do these bans actually work?

The case for banning phones

Dr. Helen Park, an education researcher at Oxford University, supports phone bans. "Smartphones are designed to be addictive," she says. "Every notification (通知) pulls students' attention away from learning. Studies show that even having a phone in the same room — even if it's turned off — can lower students' ability to concentrate."

A 2023 study from the London School of Economics found that schools with phone bans saw a 6.4% improvement in test scores, especially among students who were already struggling. "The students who are most distracted (分心的) by phones benefit the most from bans," Dr. Park adds.

The case against banning phones

But not everyone agrees. Some teachers argue that phones can be useful learning tools. Mr. Torres, a high school science teacher in Spain, uses phone apps in his classes for things like recording experiments and researching topics. "Instead of banning phones, we should teach students how to use them responsibly," he says.

And there is another concern: safety. After school, many parents expect to be able to reach their children at any time. A complete ban, some argue, could make students feel unsafe — especially in emergencies.

A middle path?

Some schools have found a compromise. For example, a school in Japan requires students to lock their phones in their lockers during class but allows them to use phones during lunch breaks. Another school in Australia has a "phone-free zone" in certain classrooms, but allows phones in hallways and the cafeteria.

"The goal is not to make phones disappear," says Principal Chen from a middle school in Shanghai. "The goal is to help students learn self-control. That skill will serve them for life."
passages.阅读理解 (B):
"Do you get nervous during competitions?"
"A professional doesn't get nervous."

Sheng Lihao, a sport shooter, is a man of few words. In interviews, he rarely says more than necessary. But Sheng has never needed words to impress the world. His performance speaks far louder than any words ever could.

One of his latest achievements came at the 2026 Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games. In the men's 10-meter air rifle final, he won the gold medal for the second time and set a new Asian record. Of his 24 shots, 19 were 10.5 or higher. He also helped China win gold in three other events.

For those unfamiliar with shooting, a 10.5 and a 10.9 may look similar, yet even one millimeter can make a big difference in this sport. The atmosphere at a major shooting event can be as tense as a pressure cooker. In the 10-meter air rifle event, the target is only 4.55 centimeters in diameter (直径). The innermost 10-ring is only 0.5 millimeters across. To the untrained eye, even seeing the center of the target from ten meters away is difficult. Yet Sheng regularly scores 10.5 or higher.

But even when he achieves a 10.9 — the highest possible score for a single shot — Sheng shows little excitement. He says that one shot, no matter how good, means nothing for the next one. Once a shooter raises the rifle, even a slight change in breathing can affect the shot. A shooter must stay calm and concentrated until the very end.

Sheng first picked up a rifle at the age of 12. He soon showed great talent and began to progress much faster than his peers. But talent is only part of what has made him the shooter he is today. His success is also built on years of hard training. "He had little of the free time that most teenagers enjoy," one of his earliest coaches, Shen Chao, once said. "On weekends and holidays, he trained at the shooting range all day, sharpening his skills."

At the age of 21, Sheng still has a long way to go. Now that the Asian Games are behind him, he may already be training with bigger ambitions in mind. What record will he break next?
passages.阅读理解 (C):
Welcome to the cyber career test! Stopping online criminals (罪犯) is one of the coolest jobs on the planet. Best of all, you don't even need to be a coding genius to get started. What really matters is having a creative mind to outsmart cybercriminals. Ready to discover your digital superpower? Take this one-minute quiz and unlock your future!

Quick question

What is your real-life superpower when you work with friends?
A. I love testing things and finding hidden mistakes before anyone else.
B. I love playing detective and following clues to solve a mystery.
C. I love gaming, building cool stuff, and making sure rules are fair.
D. I am super patient and notice small details that others miss.
E. I love sharing cool tips and explaining hard ideas in fun ways.

Your quiz results

If you chose A: You are an ethical hacker

Some hackers steal information or cause damage, but ethical hackers use their skills for good. Companies hire them to legally (合法地) break into their own websites and apps. Ethical hackers work to find security weaknesses before cybercriminals can use them. Their work keeps everyone's private data safe and secure.

If you chose B: You are a cyber investigator

Cyber investigators work like online detectives to stop cybercrimes. They watch for doubtful activities and study how cybercriminals operate. They follow digital clues like IP addresses and server logs (服务器日志) to find out attackers.

If you chose C: You are a game or app security designer

Security experts protect the games and apps you use every day. They build security features (安全防护功能) right from the start. They guard your login information, keep payment data safe, and stop cheaters from ruining everyone's fun.

If you chose D: You are a digital forensics expert (数字取证专家)

When a cybercrime (网络犯罪) happens, forensics experts examine devices like phones and laptops. They use special software to recover deleted files and trace online activity. Even a tiny clue like a timestamp (时间戳) can help solve the case.

If you chose E: You are a digital safety educator

Digital safety educators help people stay safe online and use technology responsibly. They explain complicated technological ideas in simple ways. They also show everyone how to create strong passwords, spot phishing scams (网络钓鱼诈骗), and avoid online threats.

One of the most unexpected stories of the 2026 FIFA World Cup comes from Cabo Verde (佛得角), a nation that many soccer fans may not know much about. {{36}}

Cabo Verde, officially known as the Republic of Cabo Verde, is an island nation located in the Atlantic Ocean. Its capital city is Praia. Separated from the African continent (大陆) by the Atlantic, Cabo Verde has developed a special identity.

{{37}} Blue represents the ocean and sky, white and red symbolize peace and progress, and the 10 yellow stars stand for Cabo Verde's ten main islands.

The name "Cabo Verde" comes from Portuguese. {{38}} The name translates as "green cape" in English. Interestingly, the islands themselves are not especially green due to their dry climate.

{{39}} However, the language most commonly spoken in everyday life is Cape Verdean Creole, known locally as Kriolu. Kriolu is a creole language (克里奥尔语) that mixes Portuguese with different West African languages.

For Europeans, Cabo Verde is popular as a winter sun destination with January daytime temperatures around 25°C. {{40}} During this period, however, many people come to Boa Vista, which is the easternmost island. They go there to see the turtles laying their eggs on the beaches at night — an amazing scene.
passages.回答问题:
Recently, my daughter showed me a math question. It began with a passage from the Zhuangzi: "…If half of the remaining part of a one-chi-long (一尺长) stick is removed each day, it can never be used up." It then asked, "How long will the stick be after the fifth day?" My first thought was, "Is this a math or Chinese?"

These days, many Chinese and English exercises seem to have more reading. Students have to read a short passage or a conversation, not just one sentence. In many ways, this is a positive change. After all, in real life, students don't just do grammar exercises. They use grammar to read, write, and communicate.

Math exercises seem to be changing in the same way. I once saw a math question online. It was about the dosage (剂量) information on a medicine bottle. Students were not just doing calculations (计算). They were using math to solve a real-life problem.

But not all change is good. In some math exercises, reading is becoming the main challenge, while the math itself is taking a back seat. This can be worrying. Over time, students may just try to finish reading fast. They may lose the patience to read anything in depth.

We need to ask ourselves: are we truly trying to improve? Or are we just doing things simply because others do so? For example, to attract more customers, some bakeries are making extra-long egg tarts (蛋挞). While they may turn heads, these desserts can be far from healthy.

There is nothing wrong with trying to create better test questions or become better versions of ourselves. But we should never forget why we started. If we take things too far, we may end up moving in the opposite direction.

Researchers in Australia are using a robot powered by AI to improve the way farmers raise cattle (牛). The robot, named SwagBot, has four wheels and is red. It can drive {{51}} itself and move cows from one field to another based on the condition of the soil and plant life.

Researchers say, "SwagBot is {{52}} the world's first 'smart cow'?" They believe it can make cattle farming more efficient and put less pressure on the environment. {{53}} a smart invention it is!

Researchers have added sensors (传感器) and AI systems to the robot. These systems help SwagBot judge the health, type of grasses and plants in fields and monitor the health of the cattle. The goal is to move cattle to a new field {{54}} they have damaged the grass in a certain area too much.

SwagBot can also send the information back to farmers. Erin O'Neill, a local farmer, said, "I am glad {{55}} it can find the most nutritious grass for me, especially when my cattle are about to give birth, as they need high-quality grass at this time."

For now, SwagBot is still in development. It is sort of a milestone in farming towards robotics.

假如你是李华，目前担任学校英文报网站“Advice Column（建议专栏）”的学生志愿者。近期专栏收到了四封求助网帖，请你任选其一，给发帖人写一封英文回信。在回信中：
1、对发帖人的处境表示理解；
2、给出你的建议（至少 2 条）及理由；
3、表达鼓励与祝愿。

Confused-666：Since the new semester started, I have been under great study pressure. It seems that I can never finish my homework, and my friends always seem to do a better job than me in studies. I feel totally stressed and tired. What should I do?

Miss Anxious：I really can't stand taking after-school classes anymore. My parents firmly believe that extra effort helps, but I totally disagree. What really drives me crazy is that they signed me up for a new one without asking me first! Now I have barely any time left for my hobbies. How can I prove to them that taking a break is actually good for my school performance?

Tear_89：Some classmates have been pairing me up with others to form a so-called "CP" group. I find it so annoying. Worse still, my best friend even tries to stay away from me to avoid the rumour. I feel so upset and lonely. I need some advice.

Gameboy：After school, I can't help but watch short videos or play online games on my phone. Sometimes, I even spend the whole night doing this. I feel tired in the morning and can't pay attention in class at all. I know this is wrong, but I can't control myself. Could you give me some advice?
